passage:
Vandana sat on the terrace of her house in the small town, phone in hand, watching one grey tick under her message. Arun was in Toronto, half a day behind, and his replies came when she was asleep or in class. This was the third night that week. She began to type, "You clearly don't care," and stared at it.

"Madhuri, look at this," she called down to her friend, who ran the tailoring shop next door.

Madhuri read it and raised an eyebrow. "Do you know his timetable?"

Vandana deleted the line. She wrote instead: "I miss you, and this week I felt left out of your days. Can we fix Sunday 9 pm my time for a proper call? And can we plan a visit when your term ends in December?"

His reply came at dawn: "Yes. Sorry. Yes."

qa.q: In which city is Arun living?
What was Vandana feeling as she watched the single grey tick, and what did she nearly do?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, and she nearly sent a message saying he clearly did not care before deleting it.

qa.q: What agreement in Vandana's new message could ease the distance?
qa.a: A fixed Sunday call time that suits them both, plus a planned visit when his term ends in December.

qa.q: How might Arun see the silence that upset Vandana?
qa.a: He may have been busy with classes or asleep because of the time difference, so the silence could be about schedules rather than neglect.

grounding: Shows long-distance strain where the person replaces an accusation with an honest message and plans for realistic contact and a visit.

passage: August. Gurleen moved to Toronto for her master's, and Vinita stayed in Chandigarh for her final year. The time difference was nine and a half hours. Vinita sent twenty messages a day and felt betrayed every time Gurleen took six hours to reply. One night she typed, 'Guess I'm not a priority any more,' and hit send. September. On a rare long call, Gurleen cried. 'I'm in labs all day, then working at the café. I'm not forgetting you. I'm drowning.' Vinita heard it. They made a deal: one proper video call every Sunday at 9 p.m. her time, voice notes whenever, no guilt for slow replies. November. The voice notes had become their diary: Vinita's thesis panic, Gurleen's first snowfall, the new friend she'd made in class. They had booked Gurleen's flight home for the winter break. Vinita still missed her every day. But silence no longer felt like a verdict.

qa.q: When did they agree to have a proper video call?
qa.a: Every Sunday at 9 p.m. Vinita's time.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when Gurleen took six hours to reply?
qa.a: She felt forgotten and hurt, reading the silence as betrayal.

qa.q: What deal made the distance easier?
qa.a: A realistic plan: one weekly video call, voice notes whenever, no guilt for slow replies, and a booked visit 👍

qa.q: What was Gurleen's side of the slow replies?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed by labs and work, not forgetting Vinita but drowning.

grounding: Shows a young woman in a long-distance relationship who moves from demanding replies to a realistic contact plan, shared inner lives and a planned visit.

passage: Nitin, you think long distance started with your video calls? When I was twenty-one, your Nanaji was posted in Leh with the army, and I was finishing my BA in Ludhiana. No phones. Letters took three weeks, sometimes six in winter. Once, two months passed with nothing. I was sure he'd found someone else. I wrote him a furious letter, and my mother caught me on the way to post it. She said, 'Jasleen, snow blocks roads. It doesn't block hearts.' So I tore it up and wrote instead about my exams, the neighbours' goat, my fears about the future. Every week, whether he wrote or not. When his letters finally came, eight arrived together, one for every week. We'd agreed on nothing, and still we had both kept writing. After that we promised: one letter a week each, and his leave in April. So, beta, stop counting her replies. Agree on what's realistic, tell her about your real days, and plan the next visit.

qa.q: How many letters arrived together after the long silence?
What was Jasleen feeling after two months with no letter?
qa.a: Jasleen felt anxious and suspicious, sure Nanaji had found someone else.

qa.q: What choice in Jasleen's story made the difference?
qa.a: Tearing up the furious letter and writing weekly about real life instead, then agreeing on a letter a week and a planned leave.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's mother see the silence?
qa.a: As snow blocking roads, not a lack of love.

grounding: An elder's story of long-distance strain where silence felt like betrayal, until realistic contact, shared inner life and a planned visit took its place.
